job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Review: S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment, Oct. 6, 2026)

I reviewed only the text you provided. I did not compare it against the introduced version, check cross-references in the U.S. Code, or assess the case law, so counsel should confirm the legal points before the markup.

**Top priorities for Thursday:** Items 20–21 (the 10-year sunset), 8 (no trade or import ban), 14 (Section 4 has no penalty), 4 (undefined "Secretary" with unreviewable discretion), 10–11 (exemptions that could swallow the prohibition), and 17 (no enforcement authority).

1. **§2(1)(A), "by a single vessel":** A project using several vessels that each recover under 10,000 metric tons per year falls outside the definition. Measure the threshold at the project or operator level, aggregated across vessels.

2. **§2(1)(A), "polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources":** The bill does not clearly cover cobalt crusts, seafloor massive sulfides, phosphorites, or sand and aggregate. Also, §2(3) uses "seabed mineral resources," which is never defined. Define the term and list the covered resources.

3. **§2(1)(A), volume-based threshold:** The definition turns on tonnage, not purpose, so sub-threshold or pilot operations that still sell minerals may fall outside it. Add a purpose or sale test, count cumulative and ramp-up tonnage, and cover discharge and sediment plumes, not just recovery.

4. **§2(1)(B), "the Secretary":** The Secretary is never identified (NOAA appears in §4 and State in §6). "Comparable" is undefined, and the determination has no criteria, notice, public process, or review standard. This gives an official broad discretion to exempt projects, and it could be challenged as arbitrary.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers only citizens and State-chartered corporations. It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and federally chartered entities, which are common vehicles for mining ventures. Combined with the undefined term "person" in §3(a), this leaves gaps in who is covered.

6. **§2(3), "covered vessel" (over 5,000 GT, "equipped for"):** Smaller vessels are excluded from the §4 registry and reporting duties, which creates a monitoring gap. "Equipped for" is also vague and could be read narrowly.

7. **§3(a), "engage in":** The term is undefined. It is unclear whether the prohibition reaches financing, equipment supply, contracting, services, or investment in mining operations.

8. **§3(a), no trade or import ban:** Nothing prohibits buying, importing, selling, or processing minerals recovered abroad. Foreign-mined material could enter U.S. supply chains, which weakens the prohibition's effect and invites a "leakage" argument.

9. **§3(a), geographic scope:** "In the United States" is not defined, so it is unclear whether the territorial sea, the EEZ, and the continental shelf are covered. The bill also does not address seabed areas beyond national jurisdiction (the "Area" under UNCLOS and the ISA) or existing international contracts. Counsel should assess the conflict risk.

10. **§3(b), grandfathering of exploration licenses:** "Exploration license" is undefined, and the bill does not say which agency issues it. The clause could allow commercial-scale recovery under an exploration license, has no sunset, and "issued before the date of enactment" invites a licensing rush before the bill takes effect.

11. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption:** The exemption has no cap on volume or duration, no bar on selling recovered material, no permit or agency approval, and no reporting. Because the test is the operator's "purpose," commercial extraction could be relabeled as assessment.

12. **§4(a), registration:** The bill sets no deadline, no required content, and no penalty for failing to register. "Operator" is undefined.

13. **§4(b), quarterly reports:** The bill does not specify what must be reported (tonnage, location, depth, discharge, bycatch). It also does not require public availability, verification, or a filing deadline. Self-certification carries no false-statement penalty.

14. **§5, penalties do not cover §4:** Civil and criminal penalties reach only §3 violations. The registry and reporting duties are therefore effectively voluntary. Add penalties for failure to register, failure to report, and false reporting.

15. **§5(a), civil penalty mechanics:** "Each day" is undefined, and there is no per-vessel or per-ton measure, no inflation adjustment, and no disgorgement of profits. The bill also provides no forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals and no in rem liability for vessels. The "on or after the date of enactment" language conflicts with the 180-day effective date in §8 and should refer to the effective date.

16. **§5(b), criminal penalty:** "Willfully" is undefined. The bill also has no responsible-corporate-officer liability and no express attempt or conspiracy language. Consider whether existing Title 18 provisions suffice.

17. **Whole Act, no enforcement architecture:** The bill does not designate an agency to administer or enforce §3, grant rulemaking authority, provide appropriations, authorize injunctions or cease-and-desist orders, or create a citizen suit. Without these, enforcement depends on DOJ initiative alone.

18. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate":** The duty is to try, not to conclude an agreement, and there is no reporting requirement or consequence for failure. "Equivalent to those in section 3" is undefined. It is also unclear whether the 18-month deadline applies to starting talks or concluding an agreement.

19. **§7(a), "serious harm" standard and NASEM report:** "Serious harm" is undefined and does not match the irreversibility rationale in the coalition's own framing. The bill sets no deadline for the NASEM report and does not say what happens if no report is issued, so the lifting mechanism may never activate or may be disputed.

20. **§7(b), 10-year sunset:** This is the most serious problem. The Act ceases to have effect after 10 years regardless of whether §7(a)'s findings have been made, so mining could resume automatically. It directly conflicts with §7(a)'s indefinite duration.

21. **§7(b) and §8, the sunset runs from enactment, not the effective date:** The sunset counts from enactment, but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. The prohibition therefore operates for about 9.5 years, not 10. Combined with item 20, this shortens the protection further.

22. **§8, 180-day delay:** The delay creates a window for pre-enactment ramp-up and combines with the grandfathering clause in §3(b) to increase the risk of a licensing rush.

23. **Missing severability clause:** If a court strikes one provision, such as the penalty section, the rest of the Act could fall with it or be left unenforceable. Add a standard severability clause.

24. **Missing savings and preemption clause:** The bill does not say whether it preempts state law, whether stronger state or international protections survive, or how it interacts with existing law (OCSLA, NEPA, the Marine Mammal Protection Act, the Clean Water Act). Ambiguity here invites litigation.

25. **Missing findings and purpose section:** The bill has no findings or statement of purpose and does not identify its constitutional authority (for example, the Commerce Clause, foreign commerce, or the Property Clause as applied to the OCS). Findings help courts interpret ambiguous terms and make a jurisdictional challenge harder to sustain.

26. **General drafting:** Several terms are used inconsistently or undefined, including "person," "operator," "exploration license," "environmental assessment," "seabed mineral resources," and "Secretary." A definitions pass would resolve many of the items above.

**Suggested next step:** Items 20–21 and 8 are the highest-impact fixes and the most likely to draw industry pushback, so they should be prepared first. I can draft amendment language for any of these items if that would help. I would recommend having counsel review items 9, 18, and 25, which involve international law and constitutional authority.
